title: Evaluation of the Small Punch Test: Repeatability and Sample Parameter Influence
abstract: Abstract The small punch test (SPT) is a fast method to evaluate alloys and compositional gradients across small length scales. However, its repeatability is commonly in question given size effects and sample preparation requirements. This study analyzes cold drawn commercial grade mild steels, correlating testing parameters to differences in microstructure and comparing them to the literature. The samples tested produced force–displacement curves that exhibited the expected five-stage deformation sequence. Low variance between tests proved sound sample preparation and testing techniques were used. Distinguished values of the curves were then used to develop an empirical relationship to known yield and ultimate tensile strength of the material and comparatively assessed with values from the literature. This relationship can now be applied to determine properties of SPT’s completed with similar steels. Results were analyzed further through a correlation matrix, showing a high relation between transition force and energy values of the test. Fractographic and microstructural analyses revealed ductile fracture mechanisms consistent with the steel’s properties. A heterogeneous spatial distribution of the strain field across a short length scale was observed, which emphasizes the critical requirement of metallographically homogenous structured samples for reliable data reproducibility.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Uniaxial tensile testing is commonly used to evaluate the strength and ductility of metals and alloys for having high reproducibility and accuracy in determining material properties. However, uniaxial tensile testing is destructive by nature, and it requires a significant volume of material for producing test samples. Therefore, it is regarded as costly. For example, the commonly accepted standard for these tensile tests, ASTM: E8, requires the manufacture of dog bone shape test samples with a minimum gage length of 50 mm and diameter of 12.5 mm. When evaluating the response of materials under complex service conditions, the response of localized microstructural changes or in the development of alloy systems, the amount of material required to complete a statistical analysis from tensile testing can be costly and time-consuming. As alternatives, the rapid indentation techniques such as nano-indentation and profilometry-based plastometry (PIP) require a smaller volume of material and provide an insight into the materials properties. However, the test data have significant limitations with sample surface roughness, size effect and manufacturing defects (Ref  1 ). The recent popularity developing small-scale deformative testing methods, such as small tensile tests and small punch tests, are regarded promising as they can provide a more representative understating of the material with a small amount of materials needed. The most promising of these is the small punch test (SPT), with it requiring significantly less material than small tensile tests, exhibiting less influence from size effects and it recently achieving standardization accreditation (ASTM, CEN and GB/T) (Ref  1 ,  2 ,  3 - 4 ).

Briefly on the SPT technique, it consists of punching through a disk specimen of 8 mm in diameter and 0.5 mm thick, clamped between a two-piece die. The punch can be either a miniature tool steel punch or ball bearing (2.5 mm in diameter) (Ref  2 ). SPT tests are conducted on a uniaxial tester in compression mode, and therefore, the output is force–displacement data that is used to infer mechanical properties from reference material yield (YS) and ultimate tensile (UTS) strengths. Thus, the SPT test is a low-cost alternative accessible testing method given its use of uniaxial testers, common in material testing laboratories, and widely available material data (materials databases, scientific research, etc.), used as baselines data points for empirical relationships between tensile and SPT properties.

The versatility of the technique has promoted its use in a range of materials testing applications. One of the more popular areas is in material degradation, influencing the service life of components. Altstadt et al. and Melkior et al. studied the embrittlement of radiation irradiated steel used in nuclear power plants (Ref  5 ,  6 ). Likewise, Edidin applied the SPT to ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene orthopedic bearings evaluating material degradation along the bearing thickness (Ref  7 ). Part and manufacturing process evaluation is a popular application area for the SPT in metals. For example, Lancaster et al. applied the SPT to an additive manufactured turbine blade, evaluating microstructure heterogeneities along the airfoil blade surface (Ref  8 ). The technologically similar laser cladding process was also evaluated by SPT, with García-Blanco et al. studying the mechanical response of a Cobalt clad, the stainless steel base material and the interface between both regions, giving insight into the cladding process (Ref  9 ). The advantage of SPT in evaluating narrow bonding regions is further exemplified in welding processes where SPT test samples were cut from welding fusion and heat-affected zones in both gas tungsten arc and friction stir welds (Ref  10 ,  11 ). The response of materials to thermal processing is also a promising use case for SPT’s, Miguel et al. studied the hardenability of a pipe steel through the Jominy end quench test, sectioning SPT samples along the test piece length from the quenched face (Ref  12 ). Further, Jeffs et al. studied the materials response to processing conditions and heat treatments of a laser powder bed fusion additive manufactured duplex stainless steel which was rapidly evaluated through the use of the SPT (Ref  13 ), demonstrating that rapid processing also is beneficial to materials development especially in the development of alloys containing costly exotic alloying elements. Ouyang et al. studied the high-temperature mechanical response of a custom refractory multi-principal-element alloy using the SPT (Ref  14 ). To date, SPT tests have also been applied to a range of conventional alloys including high strength steels, stainless steels, structural steels, aluminum alloys, copper, Ni-based superalloys and titanium alloys (Ref  15 ,  16 - 17 ).

Irrespective of material system, the correlation between sample condition and the mechanical performance response is important in ensuring the repeatability of the process. One influential parameter is the sample size. Matocha reported an increasing trend in the force at elastic–plastic transition ( F e ) and maximum force ( F m ) with sample thickness (0.4-0.6 mm) (Ref  18 ). Looking deeper, Lucon et al. studied the influence of sample surface roughness on mechanical response testing, noting that the elastic–plastic transition forces were independent of surface condition; however, polished samples exhibited improved correlation with tensile results (Ref  19 ). At the material level, sample microstructure’s and their size effects were determined by Wang et al., who reported an increase in strength with decreasing SPT disk size (0.5-0.2 mm) in an Incoloy alloy by virtue of its large grains, small grain number across the cross section and confinement of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) (Ref  20 ).

These studies show that the small punch test is a viable test method for evaluating a range of alloy systems with a close correlation to more established mechanical tests. However, there is a limited understanding on the wider correlation between variables and mechanical properties, with prior studies focusing exclusively on sample size and surface condition. Thus, herein we assess the small punch test on a cold drawn bright mild steel and evaluate the correlation between variables as to determine the influence of each on the mechanical response.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: The small punch testing apparatus was developed in accordance with ASTM E3205-20 and design guidelines reported by Ottosson and is illustrated in Fig.  1  (Ref  2 ,  21 ). The testing apparatus consists of two cylindrical dies to hold the sample in place and a punch to apply the test forces. The test sample is seated in the receiving die in a 0.4 mm deep recessed hole, with four M5 bolts used to clamp the two dies together at an average clamping torque of 10 Nm. The clamping die has a central through hole, 0.2 mm larger than the punch to allow for punch movement and concentricity. The receiving die’s hole is enlarged to 4 mm to accommodate deformation of the specimen sample. Fig. 1 Small punch test setup

The stepped punch is made from H13 tool steel with diameters of 2.5 and 4.5 mm. The thinner section in contact with the ball bearing is designed to displace the ball bearing into the sample a maximum of 2.5 mm as determined from the literature (Ref  15 ,  19 ,  22 ). A chrome steel SAE52100 ball bearing with a diameter of 2.5 mm was selected for SPT tests, exhibiting a hardness between 60 and 70 HRC and surface roughness of 0.05  μ m. The ball bearing was inspected after each SPT test and replaced after each test.

In this study commercial cold drawn bright mild steel bar, grades EN8 (BS 970 080M40) and EN3B (BS 070M20) were evaluated with an 8 mm diameter, within sample diametric specification. Samples were sliced from the bar via wire electro-discharge machining (EDM) into 12 samples from EN8 and 20 samples from EN3B. Each sample was wet ground with 2500 and 4000 grit SiC paper on both sides of the testing surface. The final stage was to polish the surface in contact with the ball bearing with a 1  μ m diamond solution and polishing cloth. Final sample thickness was measured at 0.5 mm for EN8 steel and 0.4 mm for EN3B steel.

A Shimadzu 10 kN uniaxial testing machine setup for compression testing was employed for small punch tests. Samples were cleaned with isopropyl alcohol before loading into the SPT apparatus with the polished surface face up and the two-piece die bolted together. A preload of 0.02 N was applied before testing to ensure no movement between the ball bearing and the sample. A cross-head speed of 0.5 mm/min was used for all tests with testing concluding at failure (20% drop in maximum force) or until a maximum cross-head movement of 2.5 mm constrained by the punch geometry.

These equations required baseline data from tensile testing. Three cylindrical sub-sized dog bone samples were produced from the same alloy following ASTM E8 with a maximum outer diameter of 8 mm reduced diameter of 4 mm and gage length 16 mm (Ref  24 ). Tensile testing was conducted on a Shimadzu 50 kN uniaxial tester at a testing speed of 2.5 mm/min.

Fractography imaging and microstructural characterization were conducted on a Tescan Clara Field Emission Gun (FEG) scanning electron microscope (SEM), with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) mapping taken at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV electron beam. Microstructural characterization was conducted on a sample sectioned along the plane of loading and mounted in an epoxy cold mount resin. The sample was ground in diminishing grits from 180-2000 and polished in two stages, firstly with 1  µ m diamond paste and finally with a 0.04  µ m oxide polishing solution with a final ethanol clean in an ultrasonic bath.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: The out-of-plane EBSD crystallographic texture map of the cross-sectional microstructure is presented in Fig.  2 (a) and (c) for the EN8 and EN3B steels, respectively, with corresponding inverse pole figure in Fig.  2 (b) and (d). In the crystallographic texture maps (Fig.  2 a and c), the grains are enclosed by black boundaries which represent > 10° misorientations between adjacent points across the line. Ferrite grains exhibit an equiaxed morphology in the EN8 steel (Fig.  2 a) with sizes 6.75-11.00  µ m consistent with cold drawn and recrystallized annealed steel bar (Ref  25 ). However, within the equiaxed grains, the gradual change in orientations, which is represented by the changes in the orientation color, indicates a small amount of deformation after the final stage of full recrystallization. The texture is presented in the arbitrary axes (Fig.  2 b) to find if there is a strong preferential orientation, which is quite low in intensity suggesting a negligible influence of texture on mechanical properties. Fig. 2 Out-of-plane EBSD crystallographic texture map (LD denotes loading direction) for (a) EN8 and (c) EN3B steel, inverse pole figure and corresponding multiple of uniform density (MUD) value for (b) EN8 and (d) EN3B steels, (e) high-magnification SEM image of EN3B steel showing Fe 3 C laths

Comparably, the EN3B steel exhibits elongated ferrite grains along the loading direction (LD) with widths between 6.72 and 8.88  µ m and an average length/diameter ratio of 3.61:1. Grains are elongated along the drawing direction with a weak crystallographic texture exhibiting a maximum MUD of 1.72 (Fig.  2 d). The refined grain size in the EN3B steel is one indicator of improved mechanical performance of this alloy over EN8 by Hall–Petch strengthening. However, more substantially the ferrite grains in the EN3B steel contain fine hard Fe 3 C (cementite) laths reinforcing the ductile ferrite matrix (Fig.  2 e).

In SPT testing, the ratio of sample thickness-to-grain size ( t / d ) is commonly cited as a limitation of the technique as  t / d  ratios < 25 (large grains) can result in mechanical performance not representative of the bulk material given limited GNDs at the low strain substructural phenomena found in the materials (Ref  20 ,  26 ). However, herein the  t / d  ratio is 45.5-74.1 for EN8 and 45.1-59.4 for EN3B steel, where results are representative of the bulk material.

sections.heading: Tensile Tests
paragraphs: To establish the correlations between SPT results and conventional mechanical properties, tensile tests were completed to establish YS and UTS factors, with results presented in Fig.  3 . Considering the EN8 steel, from tensile tests we determined the average YS and UTS values of 289.04 and 573.58 MPa, respectively. Contrastingly, by virtue of the Fe 3 C (cementite) structure (Fig.  2 e) the EN3B steel exhibits higher YS and UTS values of 413.37 and 719.44 MPa, respectively. Fig. 3 EN8 and EN3B steel tensile test curves with YS, UTS and strain at fracture error bars

Also observed in both steels, (EN8, EN3B) is the standard deviation between tensile sample’s UTS and elongation at fracture ( ε f ) is small, 9.25, 4.69 MPa and 0.18, 0.38%, respectively, signifying microstructure homogeneity, only increasing in YS (26.5, 21.1 MPa) likely due to minor surface finish differences after the machining process (Ref  27 ).

Similarities arise when comparatively assessing EN8 tensile results to those in the database for the alloy as reported in Table  1 . A 11.7% difference for the UTS, 16.5% difference for the YS and 12.01% difference in ε f  are noted between test and database results which is within specification given batch-to-batch variation in the bar material production and difference in surface conditions (Ref  27 ,  28 ). Likewise for EN3B, UTS, YS and  ε f  values lie within the material database property window, with a 38.4, 9.4 and 36.7% difference, respectively, compared to the material database maxima.

sections.heading: Small Punch Tests
paragraphs: Force–displacement curves from the SPT are presented in Fig.  4  with elastic–plastic transition force ( F e ), maximum force ( F m ), maximum displacement ( u m ) and displacement at failure ( u f ) averaged errors taken from the repeated tests. A bilinear fit between the linear elastic–plastic section of  Stage I  (I) and the plastic bending section of  Stage II  (II) was applied to determine  F e . Determination of  F e  by the bilinear fit is presented in Fig.  5  whereby the intercept point of the two bilinear tie lines (O on the graph) is transposed to the SPT curve to determine  F e  as per ASTM standards (Ref  2 ,  6 ). Within  Stage I  (I), deformation is controlled by Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio, where the slope change from yielding corresponds to Stage  II  (II) (Ref  29 ). After this, the sample undergoes membrane stretching in  Stage III  (III) from biaxial stress and an increase in work hardening contributing to the increased gradient.  Stage IV  (IV) represents plastic instability and material thinning with the nucleation and connection of voids. This stage also contains the maximum force ( F m ) and maximum displacement ( u m ) values as evident in Fig.  4 . Finally, in  Stage V  (V) the sample fractures circumferentially exhibited in a drop in the load–displacement curve with the displacement at failure ( u f ) represented on the graph (Ref  29 ,  30 ). Table  2  summarizes these findings, highlighting the small error in measured results, exhibiting consistency in sample preparation and material homogeneities. Fig. 4 Small punch test results for EN8 and EN3B steels with  F e ,  F m , um and  u f  error bars (numerals I-V denote SPT deformation stages) Fig. 5 Determination of Fe using bilinear fit of EN8 and EN3B steels Table 2 Summary of SPT results Steel grade F e , N F m , N u m , mm F f  , N u f , mm E m , J E SP , J E PL , J EN8 294.08 ± 13.91 1304.39 ± 27.37 1.79 ± 0.06 1043.51 ± 20.97 1.93 ± 0.06 1426.09 ± 42.19 1598.89 ± 65.40 991.07 ± 63.00 EN3B 194.50 ± 35.60 1152.95 ± 64.79 1.75 ± 0.04 922.36 ± 51.83 1.88 ± 0.04 1190.13 ± 93.20 1346.67 ± 110.47 742.83 ± 89.60

Applying Eq  1  and  2  from Mao and Takahashi,  β YS  and  β UTS  are calculated for each SPT sample and graphed it in Fig.  6  (Ref  23 ). The graph of  β UTS  versus  β YS  provides insight into the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relationship of the steels tested and provides an insight into the parameters for comparable steels. In addition to EN8 and EN3B steels,  β UTS  and  β YS  factors for similar steels taken in the literature. It can be observed that  β YS  values fall between 0.21 and 0.27 MPa mm 2 /N for the EN8 steel and between 0.27 and 0.47 MPa mm 2 /N for the EN3B steel. This suggests a strong microstructural homogeneity between EN8 samples with consistent elastic deformation. In the EN3B steel, geometrically necessary dislocations (GND) formation at the grain boundaries of the fine grains and Ferrite–Fe 3 C interfaces lead to local plastic deformation. These dislocations are shift into the fine ferrite grains inducing micro-yielding (Ref  31 ). Variances in distribution and location of Fe 3 C lath colonies lead to the wide difference in  β YS  values in the EN3B steel while contributing to the greater Fe values over EN8. However, there is a greater difference between maxima and minima  β UTS  values (0.093 MPa mm 2 /N) of the EN8 steel which can be attributed to slight differences in sample thickness and parallelism and less evident in  β UTS  values for the EN3B steel (0.058 MPa mm 2 /N). The scatter in  β UTS  values is the result of thickness differences between samples and is supported in the correlation matrix in the following section with a lower influence by the underlying microstructure due to the absence of work hardening effects. By comparatively assessing  β UTS  and  β YS  values for EN8 and EN3B to those in the literature, it is clear that  β YS  values for EN8 are lower than those found in the literature. However, steel grades: 14MoV6-3, SM490A and P91, fit within the standard deviation of  β YS  values for EN3B as depicted in the red band. Opposingly,  β UTS  values are greater than the comparable literature values. The P91 steel exhibits an identical  β UTS  value (0.39) to EN8, with AISI 1045 falling within the standard deviation of measurements. For the EN3B alloy, EN8 and 14MoV6-3 fit at the extremities of the measurement standard deviation. Of the literature,  β UTS  and  β YS  values none are comparable to those calculated for EN8 and only the 14MoV6-3 steel exhibits comparable values to the calculated  β UTS  and  β YS  values for the EN3B steel, 0.45 and 0.38, respectively. Fig. 6 Graph of  β UTS  vs  β YS  calculated from EN8 and EN3B small punch tests compared to literature values for; 14MoV6-3 (Ref  32 ), SM490A (Ref  38 ), SA508 Gr.3 Cl.1 (Ref  39 ), Eurofer 97 and RPV (Ref  6 ), Grade 91 (Ref  40 ), P91 (Ref  33 ) and AISI 1045 (Ref  33 ) steels

A graph representing the actual and predicted yield strength and ultimate tensile strength for EN8 and EN3B is presented in Fig.  7  and is used to evaluate the  β UTS  and  β YS  values calculated from Eq  1  and  2  and from the literature in predicting mechanical response of EN8 and EN3B steels. The average  β UTS  and  β YS  values in Fig.  6  are input into Eq  3  and  4  for each of the respective EN8 (Fig.  7 a) and EN3B (Fig.  7 b) samples. The  β UTS  and  β YS  values for 14MoV6-3 and P91 are selected for comparative assessment due to their similarity to calculated values (Ref  32 ,  33 ). Observing YS an UTS values for the EN8 steel (Fig.  7 a), it is evident that the calculated  β UTS  and  β YS  values strongly predict mechanical performance of the steel overlapping the tensile results. Using  β YS  and  β UTS  values calculated from EN3B and 14MoV6-3 steel on average overestimates YS by 112.92 and 159.20 MPa, and UTS by 54.42 and 84.22 MPa respectively. Interestingly, using the P91 β UTS  value overestimates YS by 230.34 MPa but accurately predicts UTS, suggesting considerable microstructure differences in P91 (martensite, etc.) influencing the yielding response of the steel. Observing the EN3B UTS and YS predictions (Fig.  7 b), it is clear that the SPT results overlap with tensile results, however, with a greater YS variance by virtue of the microstructure as discussed above. The closest representative YS and UTS values are obtained by using the  β YS  and  β UTS  values from 14MoV6-3, with it over-predicting YS and UTS by only 58.52 and 35.05 MPa respectively. Notably, EN8 and P91 under-predict UTS by 59.38 MPa but greatly under- and over-predict YS by 107.26 and 133.41 MPa, respectively. Of the two alloys tested,  β YS  and  β UTS  values for EN3B are more representative of those observed in the literature particularly 14MoV6-3 steel (Ref  32 ). Fig. 7 (a) EN8 and (b) EN3B UTS vs YS values calculated from Eq  3  and  4  using  β UTS  and  β YS  values from Fig.  6  for EN8, EN3B, 14MoV6-3 (Ref  32 ) and P91 (Ref  33 ) steels

sections.heading: Correlation Matrix of Parameters
paragraphs: A correlation matrix was developed to evaluate the correlation between variables of the small punch and is presented in Fig.  8  with greater values indicating a higher correlation between parameters. In this matrix, each variable derived from the SPT has had its correlation coefficients calculated with one another. The first point of significance comes from the only controllable variable in the process, disk thickness ( h 0 ). Matocha suggested that there is a strong relationship between  h 0  and transition force  F e  (Ref  18 ). In this work, the correlation factor of 0.32 between  h 0  and  F e  for the EN8 steel and 0.63 for the EN3B steel herein is relatively low, suggesting a lesser correlation between variables within samples cut at the same thickness. This is expected as there is a narrow variance between sample thicknesses of both alloys (60-61.3  µ m) which is within sample preparation procedures for thin disks, suggesting robustness of the SPT process. It may also be noted that the correlation coefficients between  h 0  and other parameters increase from ~ 0.3 for EN8 to ~ 0.6 for EN3B, a result of an increased number of samples tested in the later alloy (EN3B) and greater distribution of results. Fig. 8 Correlation matrix between small punch test factors for (a) EN8 and (b) EN3B steels

It may be noted that  F e  in EN8 and EN3B , F m  in EN3B and  F f  in EN3B exhibit a high correlation to all energy values ( > 0.8), although they are not directly included in the energy equations (Eq  5 ,  6  and  7 ). This is expected as these forces play a key role in the amount of energy required for the rest of the test. The transition force  F e  exhibits the highest correlation to energy values, as a transition that takes more force means the specimen does not want to deform, and thus more energy is required.

sections.heading: SPT Sample Fracture Surface
paragraphs: An SEM image of the underside surface of the EN8 SPT sample is presented in Fig.  9  along with selected area higher magnification imaging of the fracture surfaces. The flat outer diameter corresponds to the region for which the sample was clamped by the dies and is measured to be ~ 1 mm. The initial yielding band is examined at higher magnifications in Fig.  9 (a) and exhibits the formation of ~ 200- µ m-wide slip band, shown as highlighted ridges, denoted between the white dashed lines. These bands are observed to dissipate in intensity in the direction of the deformation tip. Slip bands are more prominent at the edge of the yield band as this is where the localized deformation occurs. This area accumulates a lot of strains as represented by the material bending and pulling, which is reflected in the change in contrast along the ridges area. Fig. 9 SEM image of the EN8 steel SPT sample after testing with high-magnification regions showing: (a) initial radial shear band region, (b) pinhole formation at the indentation tip, (c) fracture surface of main crack fracture

The center of the sample is presented in Fig.  9 (b) and exhibits severe material deformation and surface tension with the presence of multiple micro-sized pinhole defects ( ~ 12.5  µ m). These pinhole defects exhibit the onset of void nucleation and enlarge radially with stress as noted by the ~ 74  µ m sized pinhole (Ref  1 ). The connection of these pinholes leads to crack formation and subsequently sample failure. The radial crack formation is observed at high magnification in Fig.  9 (c). Micro-dimpling features are observed in high-magnification imaging of the crack surface in Fig.  9 (c). These features indicate ductile fracture which is expected given the FCC structure of mild steels.

Cross-section micrographs of the SPT sample are presented in Fig.  10 . Deformation from the ball bearing and thinning of the sample’s cross section is clear from the low-magnification micrograph in Fig.  10 (a). The sample thickness ( h 0 ) and final sample thickness ( h f ) are 503.0 and 214.01  µ m, respectively. The higher resolution image of the fracture zone (Fig.  10 b) highlights the shearing of the material where the tensile is its highest, propagating the crack through the material. Similar fractures were observed in ferrite–martensitic steels with fractures occurring at sites of strain localization (Ref  34 ,  35 ). Furthermore, the onset of material separation and void formation which can lead to crack initiation is observed in regions near the crack. These voids form from stress raisers pulling grains apart, comparable to the pinholing in Fig.  9 (c). A large area EBSD map covering the entire cross section from the deformation generated yield band (also shown in Fig.  9 a) region to the deformation tip region is presented in Fig.  10 (a) to show the stress distributions across different zones. The texture data are not presented because the deformation-induced bending of the disk led to the continuous change of the deformation axes, and therefore, the orientation data require a special way to present that is outside the scope of the current manuscript. Overall, there are three obvious deformation regions, labeled as zone I, II, and III, as labeled in Fig.  10 (c). The grains in Zones  II  and  III  still show equiaxed distribution and therefore indicate minor to no plastic deformation. Between these two zones, there is a ~ 200- µ m-wide yield band region, enclosed by two dashed lines. The grains at the  X  end of the region experienced a tensile strain, while the grains in the  Y  end experienced a compressive strain. This is obvious from the shape of the grains, showing elongations along the length and thickness, respectively. In the mid-thickness, the grains are equiaxed. Another transition of strain distribution is found between Zones  I  and  II . The grains in Zone  II  are equiaxed, but moving closer to the indentation tip in Zone  I , there is a significant rise in the tensile strain deforming grains increasing in intensity up to the rupture region. Then, under the indentation tip at the membrane stress region, the grains sustain the equiaxed shape with deformation-induced substructural features formed inside the grains at temporal high strain peaks leading to material displacement and pinhole formations in Fig.  9 (b). Fig. 10 (a) SEM image of cross-sectioned tested EN8 steel SPT sample, (b) high-magnification image of the radial fracture, (c) out-of-plane EBSD crystallographic texture map (white square region in a)

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Cold drawn bright mild steels were evaluated for their mechanical performance using an in-house designed and fabricated small punch test apparatus. The results demonstrated a strong robustness of the testing process with low variation of results across the tests. A sound sample manufacturing technique was shown from the high thickness-to-grain size ratio. Samples were therefore representative of the bulk material. Correlation matrices of testing parameters highlighted a relationship between sample thickness and transition forces ( F e ); however, microstructural differences (Fe 3 C lath colony locations) are seen to impart a greater response in  F e  and requiring further consideration when conducting small punch tests. The comparative assessment of calculated  β YS  and  β UTS  values against those in the literature highlights the specificity of these values for each alloy and limited interchangeability of values in carbon steels due to processing and microstructural differences. By obtaining SEM imagery of the fracture surface, samples were shown to have ductile failure mechanisms, typical of small punch tests completed on similar materials. The deformation strains of the small punch test are heterogeneous distributed across the disk length and thickness as identified by several transitions and zones of strains. Therefore, the sample selection is critical as it must have a homogeneous structure throughout the entire sample volume for reproducible data.

tables.caption: Comparison between yield and ultimate tensile strength values between the property data base value and experimental results of EN8 and EN3B steels
